briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Tax-Relief Momentum Builds in Michigan as National Rescheduling and Psychedelics Push Gains Steam
briefs.top: Michigan operators just got bipartisan cover on the 24% wholesale tax, with both major gubernatorial candidates now backing relief, while homegrown brands like JARS expand outward and hospitality-forward formats break new ground. Nationally, the DEA's rescheduling case has hit closing arguments and the FDA is fast-tracking psychedelic therapies, fueling a fresh wave of cannabis M&A and store growth.

local.text: Michigan GOP gubernatorial nominee John James made cannabis tax relief a campaign plank, arguing the wholesale levy <cite index="43-6">"drives up prices, gives illegal operators a competitive edge, and has already fallen far short of revenue projections."</cite> That follows Democratic candidate Chris Swanson's own pledge to repeal the levy, calling it <cite index="42-5">"not fair and equitable"</cite>, giving operators allies in both parties heading into November.

Michigan-rooted JARS Cannabis is expanding out of state, announcing a deal to <cite index="12-3,12-4">acquire Sonoran Roots and its eight Ponderosa brand dispensaries, which will soon make JARS the largest dispensary chain in Arizona</cite>.

In Muskegon, <cite index="7-10">Fields Cannary, a Muskegon development, is targeting a fall opening for its retail cannabis dispensary, with a full-service restaurant to follow</cite> — a hybrid format pushing further than most Michigan operators have gone.

Retailers are finding workarounds: U.P. chain Rize has kept growing by <cite index="7-14">negotiating cost-sharing arrangements with suppliers, splitting the tax burden rather than absorbing it alone</cite>, and statewide prices have leveled off, with the average ounce <cite index="11-7,11-8">down slightly from $62 in March to $59 in April</cite>.

Lawmakers are answering the pressure: a Republican state representative introduced <cite index="7-1">House Bill 6224 to repeal the 24% wholesale tax, characterizing it as an unnecessary burden on the industry</cite>, even as active retail licenses <cite index="7-13">dropped from 845 in June 2025 to 836 one year later</cite>.

national.text: The DEA's marijuana rescheduling case is entering its endgame — <cite index="22-8">the federal rescheduling case reached its closing-argument stage</cite> the week of August 24, putting a Schedule III decision closer than it's been in two years.

Federal psychedelics policy is accelerating in lockstep: the FDA holds a public hearing September 14 on therapeutic psychedelic use, and Compass Pathways <cite index="28-7,28-8">announced its drug showed six-month durability in treatment-resistant depression, with final NDA submission on track for Q4 2026</cite> for its psilocybin therapy COMP360.

Curaleaf keeps expanding regardless of macro noise, opening its 76th Florida dispensary in Cutler Bay and pushing its <cite index="61-2">nationwide store count to 177</cite> this week, with grand-opening events set for September 12-13.

M&A is roaring back post-rescheduling: Sunderstorm's acquisition of pre-roll brand Lime is the latest sign that <cite index="39-9,39-10">after years of stalled dealmaking, distressed sales, and defensive restructurings, cannabis brand acquisitions are reappearing in headlines</cite>, with buyers chasing brand equity again.

Hemp operators got breathing room too: the <cite index="21-5">House of Representatives is expected to take up Senate-passed legislation to delay the scheduled federal recriminalization of hemp THC products</cite>, buying the industry more time to shape real regulations instead of a blanket ban.
